records.title: Show HN: Made an open-source Lego AI generator
records.author: antelocnova
records.storyText:
Hi there :-) New on HN, first time posting.

Past year, around December, I started experimenting with making ChatGPT and Claude generate source code in LDraw language.

This LDraw is literally an "assembly" language, a low-level programming language that describes how to assemble LEGO pieces together into models, one placement instruction at a time.

When executed by specific tools, like e.g. LDView, LeoCAD, Studio... these instructions become LEGO CAD models, that can be interacted with, modified, etc.

Or, in other words: one LDraw source file in .mpd or .ldr format is equivalent to one LEGO CAD model.

So, the idea I had was: if I manage for maybe ChatGPT or Claude to generate high-quality LDraw source files... then, they would actually be generating high-quality LEGO CAD models, right?

Then, after months of iterations and trying one thing after the other... it worked!!!

Long story short: using GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5, I've managed to create a python toolset, instructions, and docs for agents in general. Now, these can be used by them to generate LDraw models.

I've packed it all as a dockerized web app for others to try and experiment, with several providers (and agents) to choose from: OpenAI, Claude and OpenRouter.

Here's a bunch of exmaples: https://anteloc.github.io/index-samples.html.

If you are curious about the internals of an .mpd model, the "what was the agent picturing on its mind", open the .mpd file that got your attention on a text editor, and read the first line under the ones starting with "0 FILE".

I'd really appreciate feedback and comments, let's see where this goes =)

records.author: edverma2
records.storyText:
pi pod runs sessions of the pi coding agent (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) in isolated sandboxes ("pods") on a server you run, in composable environments.

----

Since moving my company towards AI-native work, I have been really frustrated by the state of "agentic engineering" environments. Products by the labs (claude code, codex) lock you into a single provider for your tokens. Agnostic solutions (factory, devin, arguably cursor) make you pay per-token costs. None of these products allow you to fully customize the harness.

I've been an early and fervent user of pi, and I think it is fantastically simple and beautiful. I have felt it needs an environment for it to work across platforms with fully functional composability for teams.

This is very much a work in progress, but for my team this has been a much needed solution and has helped us tremendously. I hope you will give it a try and let me know how you would like it to improve.

records.title: Show HN: Television – an open source GUI for your agent harness
records.author: stlhood
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm co-creator of Television (https://television.run/).

Me and the team at Telepath (https://telepath.computer/) have been cooking on this and testing it with a few hundred alpha users. We just opened up the repo to the public today.

Television is a clean, beautiful place for all your artifacts. Think of it as a GUI for your agent harness, a visual space for creating and working with artifacts in collaboration with your agent. It works with any agent harness (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, Pi, OpenCode, etc) and uses whatever inference provider(s) your agent is already using. It's open source.

A CLI and lightweight server get installed wherever your agent harness is running (Linux or macOS for now). These talk to our macOS client app, which can be running anywhere (the browser is also supported with a few limitations). A set of skills tell your agent how to put artifacts on your TV's screen and modify them over time.

You use the client app as a sidecar -- i.e. you chat with your agent the way you normally do, but it can now respond by creating artifacts and putting them on your TV. Everything that ends up on your TV is yours and can be modified by talking to your agent. The entire UI, and your artifacts, are themeable.

We noticed lots of people are using artifacts in agents like Claude Code/Cowork and Codex, and lots of developers are spinning up little websites and webapps for working on projects, organizing their life or work, etc. But it all either ends up locked inside your agent's interface or as a mess of random tabs running on a bunch of ports you quickly lose track of.

We think that the future of personal computer interfaces isn't just chat, any more than it's MS-DOS. Artifacts are an early first step beyond chat. We think they should be easier to work with, and that you should own your own artifacts. So we made Television.

It's early but give it a try and let us know what you think: https://github.com/telepath-computer/television/

(BTW: we're building TV via an end-to-end fully spec-driven dev process, with custom tooling that also pulls in design and UI work. Planning to share more about that in the near future.)

I built it after 15 years as a solo freelancer on Harvest. I've been working on a replacement for the past year, and am happy to say my colleagues and I now use it full-time. In many ways it even surpasses the featureset I'd had on Harvest - it's really kind of amazing what kind of custom tooling one can build these days.

records.title: Show HN: Offline NHTSA VIN decoder, verified against NHTSA's own SQL
records.author: tuannx
records.storyText:
I ported NHTSA's spVinDecode to TypeScript and run it on Cloudflare Workers over the official monthly vPIC dump, so decoding needs no call to NHTSA (p50 about 1.4 ms).

How it's checked:

It is compared with NHTSA's own SQL functions on the original dump in PostgreSQL. There were 0 unexplained differences on 11,000 VINs. It matches the live API on 95.4% of 1,000 VINs. The rest is newer live data.

While doing this I found that spvindecode in the PostgreSQL dump never applies VinDescriptor overrides. I wrote it up in docs/NHTSA-ERRATA.md.

Limits: only vPIC is fully live. Recalls and fuel economy are partial, and complaints/NCAP are planned. Corgi is a similar project, and I haven't benchmarked against it.

Demo: https://data.ai-kit.net/vpic

records.title: Show HN: S3-Accelerator
records.author: dangoodmanUT
records.storyText:
s3-accelerator is an s3-compatible nvme cache that serves hits in under a millisecond, replicates hot objects, and stays warm when the cluster resizes.

the hot object replication was inspired by groupcache [1], but that has some pretty nasty issues when the cluster resizes

s3-accelerator fixes that by: 1) using rendezvous hashing to reduce the remapping when the cluster loses a node, and 2) when new nodes are added, asking the old parent for a give key for the object rather than going to s3

It also uses learnings from cloudflare that it's better to cache on a second hit than a first hit[2]

It also uses ktls, splice, and sendfile so byte transfer of object chunks never hit userspace. That means it can hit millions of iops, or saturate 200Gb/s network cards, while sipping on CPU

it also is parquet-aware, and has an optional SQS integration to keep the cache fresh if an object is overwritten.

S3 stays the source of truth, and you can write through the cache (it wont cache the write by default)

these features make s3-accelerator uniquely performant, fresh, and s3 costs extremely low.

It's one of those "I'll build it one day" project ideas that Opus 5.5 finally made viable.

[1] https://github.com/golang/groupcache [2] https://blog.cloudflare.com/why-we-started-putting-unpopular...

records.storyText:
A few months ago, we started getting into the problem of actually seeing how our team's AI usage and its cost actually translates into a business outcome. We recently rolled out a public version open source after a few months of pilot testing the product.

The product is UseJunction (https://usejunction.dev), and if your team is running multiple subscriptions/api from Cursor, Claude, Codex etc. this is for you to manage subscription spend, wastage and predictions.

A bit of background, we had a team of 20 people running $200 Cursor subscriptions, and some were using a few others. That was over $4000 of spend. With this tool, we were able to get that to $2600 on our next billing cycle! That is a 35% decrease. We knew that people had to be facing this problem too, so we made it opensource for the community.

All of these subscription providers leave behind telemetry on local machines, we use that to estimate usage. Soon we will be releasing a feature to attribute that spend to actual business outcomes that come from your project management tools.

Currently considering actually adding a level of control on top of observability so that teams/orgs can actually govern AI tool usage.

records.title: Show HN: A critical thinking site for kids and teens
records.author: Critikid
records.storyText:
In 2019, I was teaching science at an international school in Chiang Mai. One day before class, one of my Grade 7 students asked me about flat earth. He had heard the idea from Kyrie Irving and then spent the night on flat earth sites.

We walked through the claims and I explained why those arguments failed. He listened with interest. I was glad he'd come to me. He hadn't made up his mind yet; he was just curious. But this made me wonder if teaching the course content I was teaching was enough.

To be clear: I do think teaching facts is important. For example, when students learn about gravity, physics, and space, they're better prepared to see why flat earth arguments are wrong. The problem is we can't teach facts fast enough to combat the wide variety of misinformation and manipulation kids face on the internet every day.

This is what got me thinking that kids need to learn how to evaluate claims and information across a wide range of topics. While we can't prepare them for every false or misleading claim they might encounter, we can give them tools to assess them.

That eventually led my husband and I to build Critikid, a site for teaching kids and teens. We've been working on it for 3 years now! He does the technical work (design and coding) and I do the educational content creation.

By now, there are 5 interactive courses for ages 5-18 on logical fallacies, media literacy, emotional intelligence, statistical reasoning, and formal logic. There are also worksheets and lesson plans.

I often teach through stories, as stories make abstract critical thinking concepts concrete (and they're fun!)

If you'd like to try it, all of the courses have a free first lesson.

Are there any other topics that you think should be included in kids' critical thinking education that I've missed?

records.title: Show HN: Fakeflac-go – A tool for quickly finding "fake" .flac files
records.author: DakotaR
records.storyText:
This is my first real project; keep in mind I have no formal programming/CS background. It is hand-written; AI was only used for some conceptual questions.

Background: There's an epidemic of "fake" .flac audio files floating around: lossy audio masquerading as true lossless-quality audio. I rewrote the fakeflac.py utility in Go, adding multithreading to greatly improve performance, and increasing portability by embedding an optional WASM build of ffmpeg.

Limitations: the original fakeflac algorithm is a great starting point, but it fails to find a cutoff point with some (obviously very low quality) audio files and produces a false score of 100%. I added CLI flags to tune the cutoff detection, but future versions definitely need some work (less normalization? entirely new detection algorithm?)

I wanted a portable CPU implementation of kokoro for a project I am working on for a voice interface and found the current GGML/GGUF models were sometimes slower than python torch code. I love Kokoro for it's consistency and desired an easier way to integrate it into my projects. Focusing on a non-quantized SIMD yielded excellent performance for my targets. Theoretically portable to NEON and other accelerators though I have not tried. Hopefully useful for those of you looking for a less complex deployment of a TTS function that includes a G2P.

On the side I am exploring IPA more in depth and is where the g2p lexicon comes from. Espeak-ng involves tradeoffs on lexicon, emphasis, and frankly I just wanted to learn more about the subject. This kokoro work is largely in support of that exploration, but I figure it could be useful to somebody.

records.title: Show HN: Levenshtein – Curated Go lint rules and CI checks
records.author: johnjwang
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I've been recently building a lot of Go projects and noticed myself setting up lint rules and CI/CD and starting from scratch each time. Also, if I found a good deterministic check to use in one repo, I'd have a hard time putting that in my other repos.

So I built Levenshtein (https://github.com/wangjohn/levenshtein). It's a curated set of Go lint rules and verification checks that run locally and in CI.

The rule set is pretty comprehensive and builds on Staticcheck and other existing analyzers, with some additional rules of my own. It includes:

- Go vet - Staticcheck - Modernize - Bug finding analyzers - Vulnerability / security analyzers

There's also some fun optional checks that you can configure like:

- Semantic linters using Jev - Race detectors - Mutation testing for tests - and many more!

I've been hooking it up to my own projects and caught dozens of bugs already. For example, one finding was a test that simulated database changes with os.WriteFile but ignored whether the writes succeeded.

Would love feedback, particularly about the default rules and what should be default/what shouldn't!
